title: Draft: wsutil/nstime: Add parameter to parse ISO8601 in UTC
description:
There are three possibe cases for the input format:
1. A date/time without timezone
2. A date/time with 'Z' timezone
3. A date/time with plus/minus timezone offset.

In the third case the function iso8601_to_nstime() always
returns a Unix time of UTC plus offset (local time?).
This is counter-intuitive. It would be more natural
to return UTC.

Instead of always returning time in UTC+offset (assumed
to be localtime), add a 'use_localtime' boolean option to
configure the return.

Optionally also return the timezone offset in seconds from UTC.

[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/5606/diffs?diff_id=302794574&start_sha=caac4be6f75a6e58367402473c87be5ef7758907)

I'm a little confused what you're doing here. I believe that in all three cases what `iso8601_to_nstime()` returns is a nstime which holds Epoch time broken down into seconds and nanoseconds, and the nstime doesn't contain timezone information. That's why `mktime` is called in the local time case, and `mktime_utc` is called in cases 2 and 3, with the offset being applied in time 3.

I suppose I can see the point of returning the information, "by the way, what time zone did you parse," but the return value is supposed to be something that can later be transformed to be displayed as UTC or localtime regardless of what it was originally, and without having to care.

When you parse a time like `23:10:10+02:00` the return epoch time value can be in the UTC timezone or the UTC+2 timezone (or any other).

Any choice is valid but the caller must know which timezone is used and there is no particular reason to prefer UTC+2 over UTC, like the code does. I would argue that UTC is the better choice, if only one value must be returned.

I think the only reason to consider using UTC+2 (for `+02:00` offset in the example above) as the return value timezone is if that is assumed to correspond to localtime. This change adds a flag to parameterize that.

Isn't the return epoch time value already always UTC?
The current code, as tested by [tvb.lua](test/lua/tvb.lua#L758-787), returns `1362176088` for all of "2013-03-01T22:14:48+00:00", "  2013-03-01T17:14:48+05:00", and "2013-03-01T22:14:48Z", and `1362176040` for all of "  2013-03-01T16:44+05:30", "2013-03-02T01:44:00-03:30", and "2013-03-01T22:14Z" (and also the versions without separators.)

Are these times equal in UTC? I don't think they are, so the epoch time should be different too.
 ```
"2013-03-01T22:14:48+00:00"
"2013-03-01T17:14:48+05:00"
```
They're only equal in different timezones. But Unix time always uses UTC, so it seems to me the test result is wrong

Yes, those times are equal in UTC, that's what the time zone offset means. "2013-03-01T22:14:48+05:00" means "2013-03-01T22:14:48 is the local time in a time zone which is 5 hours ahead of UTC" - See [4.2.5.2](https://www.loc.gov/standards/datetime/iso-tc154-wg5_n0038_iso_wd_8601-1_2016-02-16.pdf):

> When it is required to indicate local time and the difference between the time scale of local time and UTC,  the representation of the difference shall be appended to the representation of the local time following immediately, without space, the lowest order (extreme right-hand) time element of the local time expression.  The difference between the time scale of local time and UTC shall be expressed in hours-and-minutes, or hours-only independent of the accuracy of the local time expression associated with it.
I think you are mistakenly thinking that the date time expression before the offset is the UTC time, along with the time zone. Is that it?
Yes. I misunderstood the spec. Thanks for explaining it, it makes sense now. I'll go ahead and close this.

Isn't the offset sign reversed? If "2013-03-01T17:14:48+05:00" is ahead (east of) UTC by 5 hours, then we must subtract 5 hours to convert to UTC, no? That's "2013-03-01T12:14:48+00:00" , not "2013-03-01T22:14:48+00:00".

Yes, the offset sign is reversed. It looks like goes back in the test (which predates the current convert function), and then the convert function was made to make the test pass instead of verifying that the test was correct. I'll fix that and the test.
Seems like commit ba85d8ef4d657f3f852eb8ee7e0cc6c2141d086e mistakenly changed the offset sign. @johnthacker can you confirm?
Yes, that was my fault, I noticed that the tests were now failing and incorrectly assumed that the tests were correct. I'll fix it.
OK that's why I was confused. Thanks for confirming.
Sorry, thanks for checking that. !5668 will have to be cherry-picked to release-3.6 as well.
